ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the relationship between robustness and overparameterization in neural networks
PROPOSAL: Empirically evaluate the tradeoff between robustness and overparameterization on MNIST with a suite of robustness metrics (Lipschitz constant, Jacobian norm, gradient diversity) and compare the performance of various neural network architectures with different levels of regularization (e.g., L1, L2, dropout).
CONTROLS: Compare to a control group of models trained without regularization and tested on the original MNIST dataset without noise.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that larger models can achieve better test error when regularized properly, consistent with the universal law of robustness, but also that overparameterized models can struggle with generalization if their predictions are highly sensitive to regular perturbations. Similar trends could fail if our regularization techniques are too aggressive and prevent the models from learning meaningful patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Generalizing the universal law of robustness to neural networks with non-Lipschitz activations
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel theoretical framework that generalizes the universal law of robustness to neural networks using ReLU and Leaky ReLU activations, which do not satisfy the usual Lipschitz condition. Derive bounds on the test error in terms of a new notion of robustness inspired by recent work on robust regularization.
CONTROLS: Apply the new framework to a simple neural network and compare the theoretical predictions to the performance of a baseline model without regularization.
COST: 5 GPU-hours (theoretical work only)
PREDICTION: We expect to see that the generalized framework provides non-trivial generalization bounds for neural networks with ReLU and Leaky ReLU activations, while the baseline model fails to achieve comparable performance. This could fail if our new notion of robustness does not accurately capture the behavior of these activations, or if the theoretical bounds are too loose in practice.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the geometric structure of near-interpolating neural networks
PROPOSAL: Empirically investigate the geometric structure of near-interpolating neural networks on CIFAR-10 using tools from topological data analysis (TDA) and persistent homology. Analyze how the training process affects the topology of the loss landscape and how this relates to robustness and generalization.
CONTROLS: Compare to a control group of models trained without noise and test their robustness on noisy versions of CIFAR-10.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that near-interpolating models exhibit a distinct geometric structure, characterized by a high "persistent homology dimension" that correlates with their robustness and generalization performance. This could fail if the geometric structure does not provide useful insights or if TDA techniques are not well-suited to analyze deep neural networks.

TITLE: Analyzing the geometric structure of near-interpolating neural networks
PROPOSAL: Modify proposal 3 to specifically investigate how the persistent homology dimension of the loss landscape correlates with the predictor's margin, as this has been identified as a key factor in determining generalization performance.
CONTROLS: Compare to a control group of models with similar architectures and training methods but different margin profiles (e.g. using a margin-unaware optimizer or manipulating the penalty term of a margin-constrained loss).
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a strong positive correlation between the persistent homology dimension and the margin, indicating that models with richer topological structure are more likely to generalise. This could fail if the topological structure does not accurately capture the relevant geometric properties of the predictor, or if margin-aware training methods do not lead to improved generalisation performance.

TITLE: Evaluating the effect of early stopping on robustness and generalization
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of early stopping on the robustness and generalization performance of near-interpolating neural networks on CIFAR-10, using metrics such as the Lipschitz constant, Jacobian norm, and test error. Compare the performance of models that are stopped early (i.e., before they reach the interpolation threshold) to those that continue training until interpolation.
CONTROLS: Compare to a control group of models that are not stopped early and to a group with the same architectures but different stopping criteria (e.g., based on training loss or margin).

However, this could fail if early stopping causes the model to lose some of the useful patterns it learned during training.

TITLE: Investigating the effect of robustness on the double descent phenomenon
PROPOSAL: Train a series of neural network models with different levels of robustness (-controlled via regularization, early stopping, or margin-aware training) and investigate how these models' performance changes as a function of model size, particularly around the interpolation threshold. Compare the results to the double descent phenomenon observed in classical overparameterized models.
CONTROLS: Compare to control groups of non-robust models and identical architectures without robustness measures.

However, this could fail if the robustness measures fail to improve the models' generalization performance, or if the double descent phenomenon is an inherent property of overparameterized models that cannot be altered by robustness measures.

PROPOSAL: We conduct an experiment to analyze the relationship between the robustness of overparameterized neural networks and their generalization performance on real-world datasets. TITLE: Establishing a Robustness Metric for Discontinuous Classifiers
PROPOSAL: We derive a new robustness metric for discontinuous classifiers, such as neural networks with argmax outputs, that focuses on the geometry of the decision boundary. Specifically, we introduce the notion of "decision boundary robustness" (DBR), which measures the minimal magnitude of input perturbations required to change the predicted class label. We provide a theoretical framework for computing DBR and show that it is related to the Maslov index, a quantity used to study the topology of decision boundaries in algebraic geometry.
CONTROLS: We will explore the relationship between DBR and other known metrics, such as Lipschitz continuity and algorithmic stability, to better understand its properties and limitations.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect DBR to provide a useful measure of robustness for discontinuous classifiers and to serve as a starting point for further theoretical investigations into the relationship between robustness and generalization.

PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal to refine the definition of DBR and establish its relationship to existing measures of robustness. Specifically, we modify the DBR metric to better capture the geometric structure of the decision boundary, and show that it is related to the pseudohessian matrix, a quantity used to study the curvature of neural networks.

Additionally, we experimentally evaluate the DBR metric on several real-world datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10, MNIST) to see if it correlates with generalization performance and other traditional metrics.

CONTROLS: We will compare the results of the DBR metric to known metrics, such as Lipschitz continuity and algorithmic stability, and also explore ablations by modifying the definition of DBR or using different datasets.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect DBR to be a useful measure of robustness that captures important aspects of decision boundary geometry, and to show promising results in correlating with generalization performance.

PROPOSAL: We provide a theoretical framework for the universal law of robustness, which establishes a formal link between robustness, generalization, and overparameterization. We show that under mild distributional assumptions, a balance between smoothness and overparameterization is necessary for good generalization, while excessive smoothness can lead to overfitting. Our framework builds on existing results and provides new insights into the relationship between robustness and generalization.

We provide a theoretical analysis of the robustness of classification algorithms, including a proof that the Bayes error rate is an upper bound on the robustness of any classification algorithm. We also show that the robustness of an algorithm is related to its VC dimension, and that a small VC dimension is necessary for good generalization. Our results provide a new perspective on the trade-off between robustness and generalization.

title: generalization bounds for finite hypothesis classes
PROPOSAL: Establish a new generalization bound for finite hypothesis classes by generalizing the Rademacher complexity bounds to incorporate a notion of robustness. Specifically, for a hypothesis class H and a robustness measure R, we prove that the following bound holds with high probability:
E[r|x] ≤ \frac{2d\log|H|}{n} + R + ε
where E[r|x] is the expected error on the test set, d is the dimensionality of the input space, n is the number of training samples, |H| is the size of the hypothesis class, R is the robustness measure, and ε is a small positive value. We show that this bound is tight and can be improved by decreasing the robustness measure R.
CONTROLS: Compare with the traditional Rademacher complexity bound
COST: 10
PREDICTION: This bound should provide a tighter guarantee for classifiers that achieve good generalization by being robust, rather than just overparameterized. However, the choice of robustness measure R is critical for the bound to be non-trivial, and finding the optimal R may require additional experimentation.

tITLE: relation between robustness and algoirthmic stability for neural networks
PROPOSAL: Investigate the relationship between robustness and algorithmic stability for neural networks, a notion first introduced in the work on excess risk bounds. We consider a family of neural networks with (sufficiently) small weights constraints, and define a robustness measure in terms of how much the decision boundary shifts under small perturbations of the input data. We prove that for deep neural networks with ReLU activations, there exist an absolute constant c>0 such that:
R \gtrsim \frac{\log(2|\mathcal{W}|)}{cdev(\mathcal{D}^{(s)})^2
where R is the robustness measure, W is the set of weights, and dev is the fraction of training examples that are misclassified by the model.
CONTROLS: Investigate how this bound applies to classification
COST: 50
PREDICTION: This result may provide some insight on the fundamental tradeoff between overparameterization and robustness, although the bounds may be loose for certain networks.

TITLE: generalization guarantees for overparameterized classifiers using robustness measures
PROPOSAL: Develop a new framework for studying the generalization behavior of overparameterized classifiers by leveraging robustness measures. We propose a new data-dependent learning rate derived from the robustness measure, which adapts to the geometry of the decision boundary. Specifically, for a classifier f and a robustness measure R, we define:
lr(f) = \frac{R}{\Delta f}
where Δ is the distance between the decision boundary and a uniformly distributed point in the input space. We show that the expected error on the test set can be bounded by:
E[r|x] ≤ \frac{2d\log|H|}{n} + lr(f)
CONTROLS: Compare with standard stochastic gradient descent bounds
COST: 20
PREDICTION: This framework should provide more accurate generalization guarantees for overparameterized classifiers by adaptively adjusting the learning rate based on the robustness of the classification boundary.

TITLE: theoretical guarantees for stable and robust neural networks using restricted isometry
PROPOSAL: Investigate the theoretical guarantees for stable and robust neural networks by leveraging the restricted isometry property. We will show that for a neural network with ReLU activations and a suitable restriction on the weights, the network is both stable and robust. Specifically, we will prove that for a network with k hidden layers and n neurons in each layer, if the restricted isometry constant δ is smaller than a certain threshold, then the network is both stable and robust. We will also provide an efficient algorithm to compute the restricted isometry constant δ.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing results on stability and robustness
COST: 30
PREDICTION: This result may provide a new way to design stable and robust neural networks, but it may be restrictive in practice due to the requirement on the weights and the restricted isometry constant δ.

We will introduce a novel measure that captures the uncertainty of the network's predictions for a given input, and use this measure to define a new notion of robustness. We will also show that our measure is bounded by the divergence of the network's predictions from the true labels, and provide an algorithm to compute it.

COST: 40
